items.summary_ai_original: Barbosa highlighted several key areas of cooperation, including emergency preparedness and response, particularly in relation to the El Niño phenomenon; strengthening Primary Health Care (PHC); improving care for noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) and mental health; the digital transformation of health systems; and access
items.article_text_original: Lima, Peru, 20 November 2026 (PAHO) – The Director of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, concluded his first official visit to Peru, during which he held meetings with government authorities, congressional representatives, and international organizations to advance shared health priorities, strengthen technical cooperation, and address urgent challenges such as dengue and measles. During his visit, which took place from 16 to 19 November, Dr. Barbosa highlighted several key areas of cooperation, including emergency preparedness and response, particularly in relation to the El Niño phenomenon; strengthening Primary Health Care (PHC); improving care for noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) and mental health; the digital transformation of health systems; and access to vaccines, medicines, and health technologies. “PAHO’s strength lies in how we can contribute to improving the health of countries across the Region. Rather than supporting a country in what it already knows how to do, it is about supporting it to innovate,” the Director said. Agreements to strengthen primary health care and prevent noncommunicable diseases One of the main outcomes of the visit was the signing of two documents aimed at strengthening primary health care and advancing the prevention, early detection, and comprehensive care of NCDs. Dr. Barbosa, together with Minister of Health Luis Dyer Fernández, Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) Health Specialist Ian Mac Arthur, and World Bank Senior Specialist Karina Olivas, participated in the signing of the Record of Establishment of the Consultative Roundtable of the Alliance for Primary Health Care in Peru. The PAHO Director and the Minister of Health also signed the Joint Declaration of the “Better Care for NCDs” initiative. “Primary health care is the best platform for advancing the control of noncommunicable diseases and improving mental health. This initiative allows us to translate our commitment to universal health into concrete action, bringing it closer to individuals and communities,” Dr. Barbosa said. “It is about accompanying countries as they integrate training, process improvements, and access to new technologies, such as telehealth, to work more efficiently and guarantee the right to health.” Health technologies and innovation to improve access to health care During his visit, the Director also participated in the 17th Meeting of the Health Technology Assessment Network of the Americas (RedETSA), held in Lima. The network supports countries in developing their capacity to assess and incorporate health technologies—including medicines, medical devices, strategic supplies, and new treatments—based on the available scientific evidence. At the opening of the meeting, Dr. Barbosa highlighted the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence, digital technologies, and advanced therapies to improve health and quality of life. He also underscored the importance of evaluating these innovations to guide investment decisions and ensure more efficient use of resources. “Health technology assessment provides the knowledge needed to guide innovation in treatments and health policies, remove barriers to access, and make spending more efficient,” he said. “Count on PAHO to support you in the important contribution you are making to ensure equitable access to health innovations for the entire population.” Dengue and measles: responding to immediate public health challenges The prevention and control of dengue and measles featured prominently in the Director's discussions with Peruvian authorities. In response to the increase in dengue cases and deaths in the context of the El Niño phenomenon, PAHO recommended strengthening vector surveillance, preparing health services to effectively manage an increase in cases, and promoting communication strategies that engage communities in preventing and controlling the transmitting mosquito. Dr. Barbosa recalled that while dengue vaccination can help prevent severe forms of the disease, it must be part of a comprehensive response that includes surveillance and vector control. Regarding measles, the Director stressed the importance of increasing vaccination coverage, identifying and actively reaching out to children who have not completed their immunization schedules, and strengthening surveillance to interrupt transmission. Cooperation with national authorities Dr. Barbosa discussed these issues with Minister of Health Luis Dyer Fernández, as well as Vice Minister of Public Health María Sofía Cuba, Vice Minister of Health Services and Insurance Carlos Espinoza, and directors from the Ministry of Health. In addition to meeting with Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Eric Anderson Machado, the Director met with the President of Congress, Miguel Ángel Torres Morales. Together with the Minister of Health and PAHO/WHO Representative in Peru, Dr. Gustavo Mery, they discussed opportunities for technical cooperation offered by PAHO in the area of digital health transformation, among other priorities. During a meeting with representatives of the health committees of the Congress of the Republic, Dr. Barbosa also highlighted the importance of prioritizing investment in health, strengthening vaccination coverage, particularly against measles, and expanding the multisectoral response to anemia and efforts to address mental health across all population groups. “Senators and members of Congress are important allies in ensuring the right to health. A law has great power to ensure that people can effectively access health services. PAHO seeks to support the country in achieving this,” he said. The Director's agenda also included a meeting with the Executive President of the Social Health Insurance system (EsSalud), Dr. Zulema Tomás, and her technical team to explore opportunities to expand cooperation between the two institutions. PAHO reaffirmed its willingness to support EsSalud in procuring quality medicines and medical supplies through the Regional Revolving Funds. The discussions also addressed the potential of digital transformation, telemedicine, and access to strategic medical equipment to strengthen the response capacity of health facilities and improve care for the millions of people covered by the country's social health insurance system. At the conclusion of his first official visit to Peru, the PAHO Director reaffirmed the Organization's commitment to continuing its work with the country, making its technical cooperation available to support national priorities and initiatives that advance more accessible, resilient health systems capable of responding to the needs of the entire population.

items.summary_ai_original: Washington, D.C., 17 November 2026 (PAHO) – The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) today called on countries across the Americas to intensify efforts to stop measles transmission, close vaccination gaps, and put the Region back on track towards elimination, as outbreaks continue to spread in several parts of the A
items.article_text_original: The Region’s measles resurgence has resulted in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States losing their measles elimination status, underscoring the urgent need to close vaccination gaps and strengthen surveillance and outbreak response. Washington, D.C., 17 November 2026 (PAHO) – The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) today called on countries across the Americas to intensify efforts to stop measles transmission, close vaccination gaps, and put the Region back on track towards elimination, as outbreaks continue to spread in several parts of the Americas. The call follows the 10–13 November meeting of the Measles, Rubella and Congenital Rubella Syndrome Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission (RVC), which reviewed the latest epidemiological situation across the Region. Following the Commission’s assessment and recommendations, which were accepted by PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, endemic measles transmission was determined to have been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico, and the United States. All three countries have therefore lost their measles elimination status. Under the Commission’s criteria, endemic transmission is considered re-established when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a country. “Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death," said Dr. Barbosa. The Region of the Americas, the first in the world to eliminate measles, regained its elimination status in 2024 after successfully interrupting endemic transmission in Venezuela and Brazil. However, the loss of regional status in November 2025, following sustained transmission in Canada, was a major setback. The subsequent loss of elimination status by Bolivia, Mexico and the United States marks a further deterioration in the regional situation and makes the path towards restoring elimination more challenging. “This is a serious warning for our Region, but it is not an irreversible setback,” added the PAHO Director. “We know how to prevent measles, and we know how to stop its transmission. With sustained commitment to vaccination, strong surveillance and effective outbreak response, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again.” Current situation As of 13 November 2026, the Region has reported 58,213 confirmed measles cases and 82 deaths, compared with 12,806 cases during the same period last year. Bolivia, Mexico and the United States have lost their status after the same measles virus lineage circulated uninterrupted for 12 months or more. All three countries are implementing measures to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response. Meanwhile, Canada has interrupted the chain of transmission associated with the outbreak that led to its loss of status and is working to regain elimination status. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world: one infected person can transmit the virus to as many as 18 susceptible individuals. It can cause serious complications, including pneumonia, encephalitis and blindness, and can lead to death. Infection can also weaken the immune system for months afterwards. The resurgence of measles across the Region reflects persistent gaps in population immunity, often concentrated in particular communities and geographic areas. National vaccination figures can mask these disparities, while barriers to health services, missed vaccinations, misinformation and vaccine hesitancy leave children, adolescents and adults vulnerable to infection. Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage, and several other countries in the Americas are also experiencing prolonged outbreaks. “This situation requires urgent action,” said the PAHO Director. “Continued transmission anywhere increases the risk of the virus reaching people who cannot be vaccinated and communities where immunity gaps persist.” Protecting those who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons, as well as babies who are too young to receive the vaccine, depends on ensuring that the people around them are protected. PAHO’s response and RVC recommendations PAHO is working with countries to interrupt measles transmission through vaccination campaigns, stronger epidemiological and laboratory surveillance, rapid-response teams and support for outbreak investigation and containment. The RVC has recommended that countries prioritize the following actions to strengthen their efforts to interrupt transmission: - Assess risks and close immunity gaps: Use PAHO’s risk assessment tool to identify high-risk municipalities and populations, prioritizing the most vulnerable. - Strengthen active case finding: Conduct active searches in health facilities, communities and laboratories every three months, and systematically document the results. - Improve classification of suspected vaccine reactions: Apply PAHO criteria, including the timing of rash onset following vaccination, and genotype PCR-positive cases to identify vaccine strains. - Adapt responses to the epidemiological situation: Use PAHO’s July 2026 Measles Preparedness and Response Matrix to guide vaccination, surveillance and laboratory activities, documenting any changes. - Protect health workers: Verify vaccination status, enforce institutional immunization policies and implement airborne isolation protocols. - Ensure timely resources: Equip field teams, remove operational barriers and coordinate government support to enable rapid outbreak response. Sustaining at least 95% coverage with both doses of the measles vaccine in every community remains essential to closing immunity gaps and preventing further transmission. National averages can mask pockets of low coverage, making it critical to reach every community, particularly those most vulnerable to outbreaks. The path back to elimination The Americas has faced this challenge before. After endemic transmission was re-established in Venezuela and Brazil in 2018 and 2019, respectively, countries worked together to interrupt transmission, and the Region regained its measles elimination status in 2024. ”Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring that every community is reached,” underscored Dr. Barbosa. Achieving and sustaining at least 95% coverage with both doses of the measles vaccine in every community, backed by strong surveillance and effective outbreak response, remains the path towards measles elimination. “PAHO will continue working with every country toward that goal. We know what works. We have done it before. And with sustained commitment and action, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again.”

items.article_text_original: As external health financing declines and public health threats persist, Africa’s flagship public health conference will examine progress, confront remaining gaps and advance African-led solutions. Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 10 November 2026: Africa is entering a defining period for its health security. As external financing becomes increasingly uncertain and public health emergencies continue to test health systems, African countries are strengthening the institutions, capabilities and partnerships needed to take greater ownership of their health future. From continental regulatory cooperation and pooled procurement to local manufacturing, genomic surveillance and emergency response, African-led initiatives are reshaping how the continent prepares for and responds to health challenges. Against this backdrop, the Fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026) will convene in Addis Ababa from 23 to 27 November, co-hosted by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and the Government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia. Under the theme “Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from Health Dependency and Vulnerability to Ownership and Resilience,” the conference will bring together African political leaders, policymakers, scientists, health professionals, innovators and partners to examine progress against continental health priorities, identify remaining gaps and advance practical solutions. With more than 30,000 participants expected, CPHIA 2026 will provide an opportunity to assess how continental commitments are translating into stronger institutions, sustainable financing, locally produced health products and better health services for communities. EVENT INFORMATION WHAT: Fifth International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA 2026) WHEN: 23-27 November 2026 WHERE: Addis International Convention Center, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia CO-HOSTS: Africa CDC and the Government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia THEME: Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty: Transformation from Health Dependency and Vulnerability to Ownership and Resilience WHAT TO EXPECT AT CPHIA 2026 CPHIA 2026 will feature high-level political dialogues, scientific discussions, continental initiatives and exchanges on African-led solutions. Discussions will focus on sustainable health financing, local manufacturing, global health architecture reform, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, pandemic preparedness and climate resilience, with particular attention to strengthening Africa’s leadership and ownership of its health systems. Among the major programme highlights are: 22 November – Youth and Women at the Centre of Africa’s Health Future Ahead of the official opening of CPHIA 2026, Africa CDC will convene the Youth Pre-Conference & Women in Health Leadership Summit at Nelson Mandela Hall, African Union Commission, Addis Ababa. The Summit aims to bring together 4,000 young people and 200 women leaders, alongside policymakers, health professionals and innovators, to advance leadership, mentorship, employment opportunities and African-led health solutions. Key anticipated outcomes include a Joint Leadership Declaration and institutional commitments to inform the wider CPHIA 2026 discussions. 23 November – High-Level Opening and Political Leadership The opening day will feature the official ceremony, the high-level launch of the AU Champions’ Roadmap on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) 2026-2030, and two Heads of State panels on leadership and financing for Africa’s health sovereignty. A ministerial dialogue with candidates for the position of Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO) is scheduled for the afternoon, providing an opportunity for African health leaders to engage on the future of global health leadership. 24 November – Global Health Architecture, Immunisation and Health Financing Discussions will focus on reforming the global health architecture, strengthening continental pandemic preparedness and advancing Africa’s manufacturing ambitions, including the target of producing 60% of its vaccine needs locally by 2040. The programme also features the Continental Immunization Forum launch, the inaugural Continental AIDS Monitoring Report and discussions on the CPHIA Health Financing Pathway Compact. 25 November – Domestic Financing, Local Manufacturing and African Cities High-level sessions will examine sustainable health financing, local manufacturing, regulation and pooled procurement. The programme will also feature the African Cities/Mayors’ Forum and discussions on primary health care, immunisation, malaria vaccines and community engagement. 26 November – Digital Health, Artificial Intelligence and Climate Resilience Plenary sessions will explore digital health, artificial intelligence, data sovereignty and the implications of climate change for Africa’s health security. Additional discussions will address early warning systems, outbreak preparedness and community-centred public health institutions. 27 November – Research, Innovation and the Way Forward The final day will feature discussions on African-led research and development, global health security and the future of primary health care, followed by the official closing ceremony. MEDIA COVERAGE AND INTERVIEW OPPORTUNITIES Accredited media representatives will have opportunities, subject to access and programme arrangements, to cover: • The official opening ceremony and selected high-level sessions. • Scientific discussions and special sessions. • Exhibitions showcasing African innovations and health technologies. • Selected announcements, reports, and partnership initiatives. • Interviews with Africa CDC experts, participating leaders, researchers, innovators and partners, subject to availability. MEDIA ACCREDITATION AND ACCESS Media houses intending to cover CPHIA 2026 are kindly requested to confirm their participation and submit the details of their assigned journalists, photographers and camera crews on or before 20 November 2026 through the link below: Media Registration Form: https://forms.cloud.microsoft/Pages/ResponsePage.aspx?id=RcblrMc-jkyxLgdyIVBd9Wa9aORvrAVHtmNH4wq5MztUMUpUNko2VERSWVVPVjdXRElIUzNWQUNYWi4u&origin=Invitation&channel=0 The information submitted will enable Africa CDC to issue official invitations and facilitate registration fee waivers for eligible media representatives. Journalists who have already registered and received CPHIA 2026 accreditation are encouraged to collect their conference badges in advance and bring them, together with valid identification, to the venue. Further information on media access, designated filming areas, interview requests, and press facilities will be communicated to accredited journalists. items.article_text_original: 15 November 2026 | Addis Ababa, Geneva, Kinshasa, New York, Rome Six months into the Ebola outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, significant progress has been made in bringing lifesaving services closer to affected communities, despite immense challenges. However, fuelled by ongoing conflict, displacement and humanitarian needs, the outbreak continues to expand, particularly in affected areas. Since the start of the outbreak, more than 11 000 cases and 5400 deaths have been reported. Children account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and one third of deaths. Seven in 10 children under five with confirmed Ebola have died. While the response has slowed transmission in the initial epicentres, 400 to 500 new cases continue to be reported each week, and the outbreak has expanded to 67 health zones in eight provinces. Contact follow-up remains below target. The high number of deaths occurring in communities, which account for two-thirds of confirmed deaths, show that infections are still being identified too late. Recent imported cases in Kenya and Nigeria underscore the continuing risk of spread beyond national borders. Delays in paying frontline health workers and responders create tension and slow the response. Six months of collective action The United Nations, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, regional economic bodies and humanitarian partners are fully mobilized behind government leadership. WHO is directing the technical health response, and the wider humanitarian system is helping enable access, logistics, protection, and continuity of essential services. Nearly 100 health and humanitarian partners are present across the affected areas, providing essential health services, including treatment for acute malnutrition. Africa CDC and WHO co-lead the joint continental Incident Management Support Team, which supports the technical health response and coordinates health and development partners across affected and at-risk countries in response, preparedness and readiness. Most of the early epicentres of this outbreak have been successfully brought under control and rapid transmission has been halted, including Mongbwalu, Nyankunde, Nizi, Rwampara and Butembo. Even in Bunia, one of the larger, early epicentres, though there is still significant transmission, the number of new cases has halved, and treatment centres are reporting low occupancy. Diagnostic capacity has grown from two laboratories to more than two dozen, while close to 2000 treatment beds are now available in 104 treatment and transit centres. Around 3000 people have recovered from Ebola, and a quarter of those have enrolled in the survivor programme. Over 17 000 community health workers and 46 000 community actors have been trained and provided with supplies to safely do their jobs. Health teams are implementing targeted strategies to support women and children, including by keeping maternal health services running. Nearly one million hot meals across 59 treatment, isolation and transit facilities have been delivered to more than 180,000 people affected by the outbreak and to support containment efforts. Surveillance, contact tracing, risk communication, community engagement and safe and dignified burials have also expanded. Almost 90% of registered deaths are now managed with a safe and dignified burial, an important step in stopping onward transmission to mourners. Cross-border collaboration has strengthened surveillance, information-sharing and coordination, while scientific research is advancing, including the evaluation of candidate treatments and vaccines. These achievements would not have been possible without the dedication of Congolese health workers, community volunteers and frontline responders who continue to serve affected communities, often under extremely difficult and insecure conditions. These successes remain fragile, however, and must be to be protected and scaled up across the affected and at-risk health zones and provinces. Violence prevents communities from getting help Insecurity remains one of the greatest obstacles to the response. Attacks and threats against response teams disrupt lifesaving operations, while ongoing conflict, displacement and movement restrictions continue to complicate response efforts. A recent armed attack in Cantine-Aloya locality led to 66 civilian deaths, including that of three health workers. Three health facilities were looted. More than 1000 contacts were lost to follow-up, and three confirmed cases remain unaccounted for. A second attack on the town was reported early on 11 November. There have been over 80 attacks on health care since the outbreak was declared. A halt in hostilities is urgently needed to protect communities and health workers, and to safeguard the progress made over the past six months. Sustaining the response The response must put the knowledge, tools and resources needed to stop Ebola into the hands of affected communities. It must take the wider view, listening to communities who have asked for help in addressing challenges beyond Ebola, from violence to hunger to weaknesses in the health system. International support has enabled the response to move from chasing the virus to controlling transmission in many areas. That progress must now be protected. Fast, flexible funding must be sustained through 2027, alongside political commitment, safe access, protection of health care and meaningful community participation. Wider humanitarian needs, including food security, water and sanitation, child protection, mental health and psychosocial support, maternal and newborn health care and support for women and girls, must also be addressed. The next phase must build on six months of progress while moving faster to reach those communities still beyond the effective reach of the response. That is essential to save lives, interrupt transmission and bring the outbreak to an end. END

items.summary_ai_original: Washington, D.C./Geneva, 11 November 2026 — Millions of women across Latin America and the Caribbean will gain access to more affordable, high-quality human papillomavirus (HPV) testing under landmark regional access agreements negotiated by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) through its Regional Revolving Fun
items.article_text_original: Landmark regional agreements will lower costs of high-quality HPV testing and help more women benefit from effective cervical cancer screening. Washington, D.C./Geneva, 11 November 2026 — Millions of women across Latin America and the Caribbean will gain access to more affordable, high-quality human papillomavirus (HPV) testing under landmark regional access agreements negotiated by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) through its Regional Revolving Funds. Unitaid supported these efforts to expand access to HPV testing and will advance implementation activities in selected countries. HPV infection causes nearly all cases of cervical cancer, which kills more than 40,000 women in the region each year. Cervical cancer is highly preventable through vaccination, screening and timely treatment. Until now, countries across Latin America and the Caribbean have faced some of the highest HPV test prices in the world. Under these first-ever regional access agreements, countries will be able to access high-quality molecular HPV tests through preferential pricing and a comprehensive support package, with participating countries expected to realize cost savings ranging from 30% to 70%. These technologies are now available through PAHO's Revolving Fund under harmonized regional conditions for all countries and territories in Latin America and the Caribbean. The arrangements expand the range of WHO-recommended molecular HPV testing technologies available through PAHO's Revolving Funds. In addition to access to testing, the agreements include implementation support, equipment access, training, maintenance and technical assistance designed to facilitate country adoption and scale-up. By building these components together, the agreements help to reduce operational barriers that have often limited the introduction of new diagnostic technologies. PAHO/WHO has recommended the use of HPV testing in cervical cancer screening programs since 2013, with updated guidance issued in 2026. However, uptake in the region has been limited due to financial, technical, and programmatic barriers. Unitaid's support to PAHO translates into expanded access to HPV testing in the region. Unitaid will also support implementation activities in El Salvador, Guatemala, Grenada, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Saint Lucia, helping countries to introduce or expand HPV-based screening programs while strengthening follow-up care for women with positive results. "Through PAHO's Revolving Funds, countries now have access to high-quality HPV testing under more favorable conditions, helping accelerate efforts to eliminate cervical cancer in the Americas," said PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa. "These agreements reflect PAHO's commitment to working with Member States and partners to expand equitable access to essential health technologies and strengthen cervical cancer prevention programs across the Region." “These agreements build on Unitaid’s global efforts to make cervical cancer prevention more affordable and accessible for women everywhere,” said Dr. Philippe Duneton, Executive Director of Unitaid. “By expanding access to affordable, high-quality HPV testing in Latin America and the Caribbean, and extending favorable pricing to countries that have historically been excluded from such arrangements, this initiative helps accelerate progress toward cervical cancer elimination while creating a more equitable and sustainable market for screening technologies.” Molecular tests directly detect high-risk HPV types responsible for most cervical cancer cases, allowing for early identification of women at risk. Compared to other screening methods, they perform better and can use self-collected samples, which can help expand access to testing among underserved populations. The ESTAMPA study, conducted in Latin America, found that HPV testing detected nearly all cases of precancerous cervical lesions and invasive cancer, while cytology, the conventional screening method, identified fewer than half of the cases. This highlights significant gaps between the accuracy of these two methods. Expanding the use of HPV tests is key to advancing toward the WHO’s global cervical cancer elimination targets – known as the 90-70-90 goals: 90% of girls vaccinated against HPV, 70% of women screened with a high-performance test, and 90% of women with lesions appropriately treated. Currently, 16 countries and territories in Latin America and the Caribbean have introduced HPV testing in their screening programs, although coverage has been limited by the high cost of the tests. The new access to molecular HPV tests through the Revolving Funds is part of PAHO’s Disease Elimination Initiative, which seeks to eliminate more than 30 diseases and related conditions in the Americas, including cervical cancer. It also forms part of the Better Care for NCDs initiative, designed to strengthen health systems and integrate prevention and control of these diseases into primary care. Unitaid’s cervical cancer elimination efforts in Latin America are made possible through contributions from the Government of Japan, alongside support from Unitaid’s other core donors Brazil, Chile, France, the Gates Foundation, Norway, Portugal, the Republic of Korea, Spain and the United Kingdom. About PAHO The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) works with the countries of the Americas to improve the health and quality of life of its population. Founded in 1902, it is the world’s oldest international public health agency. It serves as the Regional Office of WHO for the Americas and is the specialized health agency of the Inter-American system (OAS). For more information about PAHO and its work, please visit: www.paho.org About Unitaid Unitaid saves lives by making new health products affordable and available in low- and middle-income countries. Collaborating with partners, Unitaid identifies innovative treatments, tackles market barriers, and quickly delivers solutions to those in need. Since 2006, Unitaid has unlocked over 150 health products, addressing HIV, TB, malaria, women’s and children’s health, and pandemic preparedness. Every year, these products benefit more than 300 million people. Unitaid is a hosted partnership of the World Health Organization. www.unitaid.org Media contacts PAHO: Sebastian Oliel: +1 202 316-5679 / Ashley Baldwin: + 1 202 340-4025 - mediateam@paho.org Unitaid: Kyle Wilkinson, +41 79 445 17 45, wilkinsonk@unitaid.who.int
